rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad connects this verse to 42:26: its promise that God responds to believers seems at odds with wrongdoers prospering while righteous people suffer in this life.
rows.anchor: This passage connects with, and elucidates, the statement in the preceding verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse elliptically points to human greed for more and the arrogance of those who imagine themselves self-sufficient.
rows.anchor: man's innate "greed for mere and more" (see 102:1), which often causes him to become "grossly overweening whenever he believes himself to be self-sufficient" (96:6).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's response to both righteous people and wrongdoers becomes fully evident in the hereafter, not necessarily in this world, which is only life's short first stage.
rows.anchor: God's "response" to the righteous - as well as to wrongdoers - will become fully evident only in the life to come

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The life-giving rain image connects to the preceding statement that God bestows grace in due measure.
rows.anchor: This reference to the symbol of life-giving rain connects with the preceding statement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rain reference prepares for the next verse's account of creation as a sign of God's existence and purposeful activity, and of life's continuation in the hereafter.
rows.anchor: the statement in the next verse that all creation is but a visible "sign" or "revelation" of God's existence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad places the surah in the later half of the middle Meccan period and says it was revealed alongside the other six chapters of the Ha-Mim sequence.
rows.anchor: REVEALED at the same period as the other six chap ters of the Ha-Mim sequence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah's customary title comes from dukhan, the word appearing in verse 10.
rows.anchor: this surah derives its customary title from the word dukhan occurring in verse 10.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to his note on 6:62 for the figurative sense of hamim.
rows.anchor: For this tropical meaning of the term hamfm, see surah 6, note 62.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The taunt addresses the arrogance of disbelief in life after death and, consequently, in humanity's ultimate accountability to God.
rows.anchor: thus alluding to the sin of arrogance due to disbelief in a continuation of life after death and, hence, in man's ultimate responsibility to God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad points to 6:25 and 10:42–43 for related instances of people listening without understanding.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Those who have been given knowledge” means believers who know the truth or Muhammad's message.
rows.anchor: "of the truth" or "of thy message": i.e., the believers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The listeners are hypocrites among Muhammad's contemporaries and, more broadly, people who feign reverence for the Qur'an while inwardly refusing to admit meaning in it.
rows.anchor: who pretend to approach the Qur'anic message with a show of "reverence" but are in their innermost unwilling to admit that there is any sense in it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sealing of these listeners' hearts results from their following their own desires.
rows.anchor: is a consequence of their "following but their own lusts".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad glosses taqwahum as God-consciousness given to those who are guided.
rows.anchor: Lit., "and gives them their God-consciousness (taqwahum)".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad reports the consensus of most authorities that the surah was revealed in 9 AH.
rows.anchor: REVEALED, in the consensus of most of the au thorities, in the year 9 H.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah treats social ethics, opening with reverence for the Prophet and, by implication, righteous community leaders.
rows.anchor: Beginning w ith the reverence due to the Prophet and - by implication - to the righteous leaders

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discourse moves toward the brotherhood of believers and, in the widest sense, the brotherhood of all humanity.
rows.anchor: the principle of the brotherhood of all believe rs (verse 10) and, in its widest sense, the brotherhood of all mankind (verse 13)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing passage distinguishes genuine faith from merely outward observance of religious forms.
rows.anchor: The conc luding passage (verses 14 ff.) points out the difference between true faith and a mere outward observance of religious formalities.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The title comes from the word al-hujurat in verse 4.
rows.anchor: The title is derived from the mention of the word al-hujurat in verse 4.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following Zamakhshari, Razi, and Baydawi, Asad reads this as each person's origin in a father and mother, with shared biological origins implying equal human dignity.
rows.anchor: father and a mother" (Zamakhsharl, Razi, Baydiwl) - implying that this equality

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Zamakhshari explains the purpose of human groups as recognizing that all people belong to one human family without inherent superiority.
rows.anchor: without any inherent superiority of one over another (Zamakhshari).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This teaching connects with the previous two verses' exhortation to respect and safeguard one another's dignity.
rows.anchor: This connects with the exhortation, in the preceding two verses, to respect and safeguard each other's dignity.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human differences should deepen mutual understanding and appreciation of shared humanity; Asad condemns racial, national, and tribal prejudice, citing the Prophet's explicit condemnation.
rows.anchor: is meant to foster rather than to diminish their mutual desire to understand and appreciate the essential human oneness underlying their outward differentiations

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: A hadith fragment cited by Tirmidhi and Abu Da'ud on Abu Hurayrah's authority says God removed pagan pride in ancestry; people are believers mindful of God or sinners, and all descend from Adam, made of dust.
rows.anchor: the Prophet said: "Behold, God has removed from you the arrogance of pagan ignorance (1ahiliyyah) with its boast of ancestral glories.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad contrasts this qarin with the moral consciousness or reason in 50:23: here it is the sinner's instinctive, unrestrained appetites (sa'iq), often symbolized by shaytan; he compares 41:25 and 43:36 and cites Razi on 14:22.
rows.anchor: complex of the sinner's instinctive urges and inordinate, unrestrained appetitites summarized in the term sa'iq

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun “him” or “it” refers to a person's faculty of conscious, controlling reason.
rows.anchor: referring to man's faculty of conscious, controlling reason (shahid).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Evil impulses gain ascendancy only when the conscious mind strays from moral truths; this explains the point of verses 24–25.
rows.anchor: man's evil impulses and appetites cannot gain ascendancy unless his conscious mind goes astray from moral verities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad places the surah most probably in the latter half of the Meccan period, while reporting another view that it followed surah 32 immediately.
rows.anchor: revealed most probably in the la ter half of the Mecca period (according to some authorities, immediately after surah 32)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah takes its name from its mention of Mount Sinai in verse 1.
rows.anchor: takes its designation from the mention of Mount Sinai (at-tur) in verse 1.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to note 150 on 7:184 for this description of Muhammad.
rows.anchor: See note 150 on 7:184.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mighty one who taught Muhammad is the Angel of Revelation, Gabriel.
rows.anchor: the Angel of Revelation, Gabriel.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase alludes both to the angel's exceptional manifestation in true form and to the content of revelation generally.
rows.anchor: allusion to the exceptional manifestation of the angel "in his true shape and nature"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even chosen prophets do not receive the ultimate mysteries of existence, life and death, creation's purpose, or the universe's nature.
rows.anchor: even to His chosen prophets God does not entirely unveil the ultimate mysteries of existence, of life and death

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The one seen a second time was the angel manifested in his true shape and nature.
rows.anchor: he saw the angel "manifested in his true shape and nature".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad identifies the lote-tree scene with Muhammad's mystic experience of the Ascension (mi'raj).
rows.anchor: on the occasion of his mystic experience of the "Ascension" (mi'raj).

rows.speaker: Raghib
rows.claim: Raghib takes the leafy lote tree as a symbol of paradise's shade, meaning spiritual peace and fulfillment.
rows.anchor: Raghib suggests that owing to the abundance of its leafy shade, the sidr or sidrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term al-muntaha suggests that God sets a limit to created knowledge: humans cannot grasp ultimate reality, even in paradise, which God reserves for Himself.
rows.anchor: God has set a definite limit to all knowledge accessible to created beings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad glosses the phrase as the total extent or goal of their knowledge.
rows.anchor: Lit., "that is their sum-total [or "goal"] of knowledge".

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Asad bases his rendering of 53:33–34, including its bracketed interpretive insertions, on Razi's reading that the passage returns to an earlier theme; the excerpt cuts off before identifying the verses.
rows.anchor: Razi's convincing interpretation of this passage as a return to the theme touched upon in verses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The grudging, limited giving prompts the question of how the person can be sure there is no afterlife or judgment.
rows.anchor: How can he be so sure that there is no life in the hereafter, and no judgment?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad cross-references 2:124 and says Moses and Abraham exemplify how prophets throughout history conveyed enduring ethical truths.
rows.anchor: Cf. 2:124 and the corresponding note 100. It is obvious that the names of Abraham and Moses are cited here only by way of example
